ideas.title: Thistlewood Market
ideas.concept: A woodland-critter trading game where the goods you can take are shaped like real polyomino pieces (single squares, dominoes, L-trominoes, 2x2 blocks) that must physically slot into pre-cut recesses on your own stall tray. On your turn you feel the scarcity bite as recess shapes fill up and half the market row becomes untakeable for you even though it's still full of tiles.
ideas.differentiation: Base mechanic is grid tile-drafting as in Kingdomino/Calico/Azul (confirmed live: Kingdomino drafts dominoes to a free 5x5 grid, Calico drafts hexes to a free personal quilt board, Azul drafts colored tiles to a free pattern-line board). The twist: instead of a free grid where any tile can go anywhere legal, each player's tray has a FIXED, non-negotiable set of pre-cut recesses of specific shapes (4 single, 4 domino, 3 L-tromino, 1 2x2) decided at manufacture, not at setup or by player choice, so a tile you can't currently place is a tile you flatly cannot take that turn regardless of strategy — this shape-locked scarcity mechanic (searched: 'set collection drafting game tiles placed into fixed slotted grid tray' plus Kingdomino/Calico/Azul/Gorinto individually) was not found in any shipped title, which all use open/free grids.
ideas.rules: 2-4 players. SETUP: Place the central market board. Shuffle all 60 goods tiles (20 single 1x1, 20 domino 1x2, 12 L-tromino, 8 2x2 blocks) into the draw tumbler. Draw 6 tiles blind and place one in each of the 6 market row pockets, face up. Each player takes an empty stall tray (12 fixed recesses: 4 single, 4 domino, 3 L-tromino, 1 2x2) and a score marker on space 0. TURN (clockwise): Take exactly one tile from the market row and immediately press it into any currently-open recess on your own tray whose shape matches that tile's shape. If no open recess on your tray matches any tile currently in the market row, you instead discard the leftmost market tile to the box and draw one replacement tile from the tumbler into that pocket; your turn then ends with no tile taken. After a successful placement, refill the emptied market pocket from the tumbler. GOODS VALUES: each tile shows an engraved goods icon (fish/cloth/grain) and a point value 1-4. END: when the tumbler is empty and the market row cannot be refilled, finish the current round. SCORING: sum all point values on your placed tiles; +3 for each of the 4 recess categories you filled completely; +5 if all 12 recesses are filled. Highest total wins; ties broken by most distinct goods icons represented on your tray.
ideas.components: 1 central market board, 300x200x6mm flat rectangular tan PLA board with 6 circular pockets (30mm dia x 4mm deep) in a row and a 30-space oval score track engraved around the border. 4 stall trays, 150x100x8mm flat rectangular PLA boards in 4 colors (red/blue/green/yellow), each with 12 fixed recesses: 4x 20x20x3mm square, 4x 20x40x3mm domino, 3x L-shaped triple-square recess (three 20mm squares joined, 3mm deep), 1x 40x40x3mm square. 60 goods tiles as engraved flat chips sized 0.3mm under their matching recess: 20x 19.7x19.7x5mm, 20x 19.7x39.7x5mm, 12x L-tromino 5mm thick, 8x 39.7x39.7x5mm, in 3 alternating flat colors (blue/tan/yellow) per goods type with engraved pip values 1-4. 1 draw tumbler: opaque cylindrical drum 100mm dia x 80mm tall with a 35mm dia snap-fit flip lid for blind drawing. 4 score markers, 15x15x15mm pyramids, one per player color. 1 lidded box, 320x220x60mm, brown PLA.
ideas.producibility_notes: 10 distinct part types (board, 4 trays x1 shape family each, 4 tile-shape families x3 colors, tumbler, 4 markers, box) and 7 total colors — flags the 'high part-type/color-count fidelity risk' pattern, so this idea was deliberately NOT chosen as a build pick even though every individual part is simple flat/prismatic geometry with no joints besides one snap-fit lid (0.5mm clearance friction snap, proven joint class). All recess-to-tile clearances are stated at 0.3mm. No feature under 1mm.
ideas.prompt: Product photo of a wooden-toned tabletop board game called Thistlewood Market: a tan rectangular game board with six circular tile pockets along the top edge, surrounded by four colorful rectangular player trays (red, blue, green, yellow) each with a grid of differently-shaped carved recesses, some filled with small engraved goods tiles showing fish, cloth, and grain icons in blue, tan, and yellow. A round opaque wooden drum with a flip lid sits beside the board. A brown cardboard-style lidded box with woodland critter art stands behind the arrangement, warm studio lighting, shallow depth of field.

ideas.title: Cipher Row
ideas.concept: A two-player code-breaking duel where the Codemaker can trade certainty for advantage: reveal a slot's true color up front and lock it under a clear snap-cap so the Breaker can never be fooled about it, in exchange for bonus points if the Breaker still fails. The Breaker has bribe tokens to force extra reveals, so every game becomes a running negotiation over how much information is worth.
ideas.differentiation: Base game is Mastermind (confirmed: classic 4-peg hidden-code, feedback-peg deduction game, still sold as Mastermind and multiple clones like GOTHINK Code Breaker). Searched 'code breaking peg board game with lockable ward pegs blocking guess slots' plus 'Cipher Row board game' directly: results returned only standard Mastermind/Code Breaker products and unrelated games named Cipher (a word-guessing party game, a Fire Emblem card game) — none feature a voluntary partial-code-reveal-for-bonus-points mechanic with a snap-on transparent lock cap and a bribe-token economy for the guesser. Standard Mastermind is strictly full-secrecy; this twist adds a resource-trade layer absent from it and from the searched clones.
ideas.rules: 2 players, alternating Codemaker/Breaker roles across 2 rounds (plus a tiebreak 3rd round if scores are equal). SETUP: Codemaker takes 40 code pegs (6 colors) behind the fixed privacy wall on the code board and secretly builds a 4-peg code in the 4 hidden slots (colors may repeat). Before finalizing, the Codemaker may choose 0-2 of the 4 slots to REVEAL: for a revealed slot, place that slot's true-colored peg face-up in that slot (visible to the Breaker) and snap a clear ward cap over it, physically locking it in place for the rest of the round. Breaker takes 5 bribe tokens. TURN: Breaker fills a guess row of 4 pegs (any colors, must match already-revealed locked slots in their fixed positions). Codemaker gives feedback with small pegs: 1 black feedback peg per correct-color-correct-slot, 1 white feedback peg per correct-color-wrong-slot. At any point the Breaker may spend 1 bribe token to force the Codemaker to reveal-and-lock one additional currently-hidden slot immediately (same snap-cap procedure), which then also becomes a required fixed value in all future guess rows. END OF ROUND: Breaker wins the round if the full code is guessed correctly within 8 guess rows; otherwise Codemaker wins. SCORING: if Breaker wins, they score (9 minus rows used) minus 1 point per bribe token spent; if Codemaker wins, they score 3 points per slot that was NEVER revealed (voluntarily or via bribe) during that round. Roles swap each round. After all rounds, highest total score wins; a tie replays one more round.
ideas.components: 1 code board, 220x100x8mm flat navy PLA board with an upright privacy wall (100x40x30mm) fixed across its middle, 4 code-slot holes (8mm dia x 6mm deep) on the Codemaker's side, and 8 rows of 4 guess-slot holes (8mm dia x 6mm deep) plus 8 adjacent rows of 4 small feedback-peg holes (3mm dia x 3mm deep) on the Breaker's side. 40 code pegs, cylinders 8mm dia x 20mm tall, in 6 colors (red/blue/green/yellow/orange/purple PLA). 32 feedback pegs, cylinders 4mm dia x 8mm tall, in 2 colors (white/black PLA). 6 ward caps, clear PLA hollow cylinders 9mm inner dia x 10mm tall, snap-fit over an 8mm code peg. 6 bribe tokens, flat discs 10mm dia x 3mm thick, gold PLA, stored in a small tray 60x20x5mm with 6 matching circular recesses (10mm dia x 2mm deep). 1 lidded box, 250x140x50mm, navy PLA.
ideas.producibility_notes: 5 part types total (board, 2 peg types, ward caps, bribe tray+tokens) and a low, controlled color count (6 code colors + 2 feedback colors + gold + navy + clear). Every peg-to-hole fit uses the proven peg-in-hole joint at an explicit 0.3mm clearance (8.3mm holes for 8mm pegs, 4.3mm holes for 4mm pegs). The one non-obvious joint is the ward cap snap-fit, stated as a hollow clear cylinder with a 9mm ID over an 8mm peg (1mm/0.5mm-radius interference band), a simple friction snap with no feature under 1mm. No hidden dual-depth holes are used — every hole is a single fixed depth, removing the tolerance risk of a layered/hidden-peg design.
ideas.prompt: Product photo of a two-player deduction board game called Cipher Row: a navy blue rectangular board with a raised center wall dividing a secret code area (4 colorful pegs, one topped with a clear snap cap) from eight rows of guess holes filled with red, blue, green, yellow, orange and purple cylindrical pegs, small black and white feedback pegs beside each row, a small tray of gold coin-like bribe tokens to the side, and a navy lidded box with a magnifying-glass and cipher motif in the background, dramatic side lighting on a dark wood table.
ideas.cad_prompt: Model a tabletop deduction game kit as separate rigid PLA parts, all edges filleted 0.5mm: PART A 'code board': flat rectangular board 220mm long x 100mm wide x 8mm thick, navy blue color. On top of it stands an integral upright wall 100mm long x 30mm tall x 4mm thick positioned 40mm from one short edge, dividing the board into a 40mm-deep Codemaker zone and a 180mm-deep Breaker zone. In the Codemaker zone, 4 cylindrical holes each 8mm diameter x 6mm deep, spaced 15mm apart in a single row. In the Breaker zone, 8 rows spaced 20mm apart, each row containing 4 cylindrical holes 8mm diameter x 6mm deep spaced 15mm apart, plus directly beside each row 4 small cylindrical holes 3mm diameter x 3mm deep spaced 6mm apart. PART B 'code peg' (produce 40 copies total, split evenly into 6 colors: red, blue, green, yellow, orange, purple): solid cylinder 8mm diameter x 20mm tall with a rounded top. PART C 'feedback peg' (produce 32 copies total, 16 white and 16 black): solid cylinder 4mm diameter x 8mm tall. PART D 'ward cap' (produce 6 copies, clear/transparent PLA): hollow open-bottom cylinder, outer diameter 11mm, inner bore diameter 9mm (giving a 1mm press-fit interference band against an 8mm Part B peg wrapped by no additional layer, i.e. designed to snap over a Part B peg already seated in a Part A hole), height 10mm, wall thickness 1mm, with a small internal lip 0.5mm tall at the bottom rim to create a positive snap-click retention. PART E 'bribe token tray': flat rectangular tray 60mm x 20mm x 5mm thick, gold color, with 6 circular recesses 10mm diameter x 2mm deep in a single row. PART F 'bribe token' (produce 6 copies, gold color): flat disc 9.7mm diameter x 3mm thick (0.3mm clearance to Part E recesses). PART G 'game box': open-top rectangular tray 250mm x 140mm x 45mm deep, wall thickness 3mm, navy blue. PART H 'box lid': rectangular shell 252mm x 142mm x 8mm deep sized to friction-fit over Part G's opening with 0.4mm clearance. Assembly: all pegs (B, C) press-fit into board holes (Part A) with 0.3mm clearance, a standard friction peg-in-hole joint; ward caps (D) snap over seated Part B pegs; all other parts sit loose in the box at final packing; lid (H) friction-fits over box (G) at 0.4mm clearance.

ideas.title: Threshing Floor
ideas.concept: A tight 6-round worker-placement game where every worker you send to the fields comes back with grain discs that slide onto your own fixed stacking post at the center of the board, so your progress is a physically visible tower everyone can see and race against. A turn feels like a quick tactical squeeze: which two fields will out-produce whatever your neighbors are about to grab first.
ideas.differentiation: Searched 'worker placement game with stacking grain silo chip pieces on hex farm tiles' and the plain title 'Silo Stack'/'Threshing Floor' board game: results surfaced only unrelated products (a token storage organizer called Token Silo, an abstract stacking-checkers game called Silo by Mark Steere with no worker placement or farming theme, and an area-control game SILOS with no stacking component). No shipped worker-placement game was found where collected resources are physically slid onto a fixed personal scoring post as the core visible-progress mechanic (as opposed to tracked on paper/a numbered track); this combination of worker placement + a rigid non-tipping resource-stacking post is not documented in any result.
ideas.rules: 2-4 players, 6 rounds. SETUP: place the single fixed farm board (7 hex field spaces of 3 types: wheat=3 grain, barley=2 grain, oat=1 grain, each hex has 3 divots for workers, no exclusivity limit beyond 3 workers per hex). Each player takes 4 worker pegs in their color and stands at their own fixed stacking post (integral to the board, one per player position). 60 grain discs form a general supply. Round marker starts at round 1. ROUND STRUCTURE: (1) Placement — in turn order, players alternate placing one worker peg at a time into any open divot on any hex until all workers (4 per player) are placed; a hex may hold up to 3 workers total from any combination of players. (2) Collection — simultaneously, every player sums the grain value of all hexes where they have at least one worker (count the hex's value once per worker they have there, so 2 of your workers on a wheat hex = 6 grain) and takes that many grain discs from supply, sliding them down over their personal stacking post. (3) Reset — all workers return to hand; rotate the round marker one detent to advance the round number. After round 6, the game ends. SCORING: each player's score equals the number of discs stacked on their post, plus 1 bonus point per disc by which their stack exceeds the next-tallest opponent's stack (capped at 10 bonus points). Highest score wins; ties broken by most grain collected in the final round.
ideas.components: 1 farm board, 260mm diameter flat circular PLA board (tan/green) with 7 raised hex cells (50mm flat-to-flat) each bearing 3 shallow divots (8mm dia x 2mm deep) for worker pegs, plus 4 fixed cylindrical stacking posts (15mm dia x 60mm tall) rigidly molded upright at 4 positions near the board's rim, one per player, plus a rotating round-tracker disc (30mm dia, 6 printed detent notches) on a fixed 4mm center pivot pin near the board edge. 16 worker pegs, small cone-topped pegs 12mm base dia x 25mm tall, 4 each in red/blue/green/yellow PLA. 60 grain discs, flat tan PLA rings 25mm outer dia x 16mm inner bore dia x 4mm thick (0.5mm clearance over the 15mm posts). 1 lidded box, 280x280x70mm, green PLA.
ideas.producibility_notes: 5 part types (board with integral posts, worker pegs, grain discs, round tracker, box) and 5 total colors (4 player colors + tan). Zero player-facing tolerance risk in the stacking mechanic: grain discs have a 16mm bore over a rigid 15mm post that is integral to the board (not a separate dowel needing alignment), so discs cannot topple or misalign — this is a deterministic tally mechanism, not a balance/dexterity mechanic, sidestepping the gravity/friction-fit failure pattern entirely. The only rotating joint is the round tracker disc on its integral pivot pin, the proven pivot-disc-with-detents type, stated at a standard fit. No feature under 1mm.
ideas.prompt: Product photo of a farming board game called Threshing Floor: a round tan and green board with seven hexagonal field tiles arranged in a flower pattern, small cone-shaped worker pegs in red, blue, green and yellow standing on the fields, and near the board's edge four tall vertical pegs each with a neat stack of pale golden grain-disc rings threaded onto them at different heights, a small round rotating dial tracker to one side, and a green lidded box with harvest wheat-sheaf artwork behind the scene, warm golden-hour lighting.
ideas.cad_prompt: Model a tabletop worker-placement game kit as separate rigid PLA parts, all edges filleted 0.5mm: PART A 'farm board': flat circular disc 260mm diameter x 8mm thick, tan/green color, with 7 raised hexagonal cells each 50mm flat-to-flat x 3mm tall protruding from the top face arranged in a flower pattern (1 center hex surrounded by 6), each hex bearing 3 shallow divots 8mm diameter x 2mm deep for worker pegs. Additionally, molded as one rigid piece with Part A, 4 vertical cylindrical posts each 15mm diameter x 60mm tall, standing perpendicular to the board at 4 positions spaced evenly near the board's outer rim, and one integral vertical pivot pin 4mm diameter x 8mm tall located at a 5th position near the rim for the round tracker. PART B 'round tracker disc': flat disc 30mm diameter x 5mm thick with a center through-hole 4.3mm diameter (0.3mm clearance over Part A's pivot pin) and 6 shallow notches 2mm wide cut into its outer edge at 60-degree intervals, printed with numbers 1-6 around its face. PART C 'worker peg' (produce 16 copies total, 4 each in red, blue, green, yellow): a cone shape with a 12mm diameter circular base tapering to a rounded point, 25mm tall overall, with a flat bottom. PART D 'grain disc' (produce 60 copies, tan color): a flat ring, 25mm outer diameter, 16mm inner bore diameter, 4mm thick. PART E 'game box': open-top rectangular tray 280mm x 280mm x 65mm deep, wall thickness 3mm, green color. PART F 'box lid': rectangular shell 282mm x 282mm x 8mm deep sized to friction-fit over Part E's opening with 0.4mm clearance. Assembly: Part B mounts on Part A's integral pivot pin with 0.3mm clearance, free to rotate by hand, held on by a slight friction fit; Part D rings slide freely down over Part A's integral posts (16mm bore over 15mm post, 0.5mm clearance, no other retention needed since the post is rigid and vertical); worker pegs (C) sit loose in board divots; lid (F) friction-fits over box (E) at 0.4mm clearance.

ideas.title: Market Wheel
ideas.concept: A drafting game where you commit to a numbered slot on a shared rotating goods wheel before it spins, meaning you're betting on where your target tile will END UP, not what's sitting in front of you right now. A turn feels like a blind bluff crossed with a memory puzzle, since everyone secretly points at a position and only the reveal-after-spin tells you what you actually won.
ideas.differentiation: Base mechanic is simultaneous card/tile drafting as in Sushi Go (searched: pass-and-pick hand drafting) and 7 Wonders. Searched 'rotating wheel disc reveals different goods each round for card drafting' and the plain title 'Market Wheel board game': no shipped game combining simultaneous secret slot-selection with a physical post-selection rotation of the draft pool was found (results returned only unrelated wheel-spinner party games like Wheel of Fortune and Big Wheel, none of which involve drafting goods tiles). The specific twist — players claim a POSITION on the wheel before a random rotation amount is applied, so the claimed position's contents change between selection and reveal — is not documented in any searched result.
ideas.rules: 3-4 players, 8 rounds. SETUP: shuffle the 48 goods tiles (4 types x 12) and place one face-up in each of the wheel's 8 pockets. Each player takes a personal claim board (with a 3-sided privacy lip) and 1 claim peg. TURN (per round): (1) Secretly and simultaneously, each player places their claim peg into the numbered divot (1-8) on their own claim board matching the wheel pocket they want; boards are shielded by their lips so opponents cannot see the choice. (2) Once everyone signals ready, one player rolls the rotation die (faces: 1,1,2,2,3,3) and rotates the wheel that many pockets clockwise. (3) Reveal: for each player, look at whichever pocket their chosen NUMBER now physically occupies after rotation (not the number's original contents) — that tile is theirs; move it to their personal supply. If two or more players chose the same number, none of them receive that tile; instead each of those players draws one random tile from the face-down bonus pool. (4) Refill every emptied wheel pocket with a new tile from the shuffled draw pile. SCORING (after 8 rounds): sum the printed value (1-4) of all tiles you collected, plus 4 bonus points for each complete set of one-of-each of the 4 goods types (sets counted greedily, tiles can only be used in one set). Highest score wins.
ideas.components: 1 base board, 220x220x15mm flat square PLA board with a central 8mm diameter pivot pin. 1 wheel disc, 200mm diameter x 8mm thick PLA disc mounted on the pivot pin, with 8 pie-slice pockets (20x40x5mm recesses) around its rim holding goods tiles. 48 goods tiles, rectangular engraved chips 18x38x4mm in 4 colors (one per goods type) with printed values 1-4. 4 personal claim boards, 100x60x4mm flat mats in 4 player colors, each with 8 numbered divots (6mm dia x 4mm deep) and a 3-sided raised privacy lip (15mm tall) on 3 edges. 4 claim pegs, cone pegs 10mm base dia x 15mm tall, one per player color. 1 rotation die, 16mm cube, faces 1,1,2,2,3,3. 1 lidded box, 260x260x60mm, teal PLA.
ideas.producibility_notes: 6 part types (base+wheel counted together as the pivot assembly, tiles, claim boards, claim pegs, die, box) and moderate color count (4 goods colors + 4 player colors + teal). The wheel-on-pin is the proven pivot-disc joint, stated with an 8.3mm bore in the wheel over an 8mm integral pin (0.3mm clearance, simple rotation, no snap detents needed since the 8 pockets are large enough to align by eye against a fixed rim arrow). No feature under 1mm; the smallest functional feature is the 6mm claim divots.
ideas.prompt: Product photo of a board game called Market Wheel: a square teal base board with a large round wooden-look wheel mounted on top divided into 8 colorful pockets holding rectangular goods tiles in orange, blue, purple and green, four small rectangular player mats with raised side walls and colored cone pegs arranged around it, a single die showing pip faces nearby, and a teal lidded box with a stylized marketplace wheel illustration in the background, bright even studio lighting.
ideas.cad_prompt: Model a tabletop drafting game kit as separate rigid PLA parts, all edges filleted 0.5mm: PART A 'base board': flat square board 220mm x 220mm x 15mm thick, teal color, with a vertical integral cylindrical pivot pin at its exact center, 8mm diameter x 12mm tall. PART B 'wheel disc': flat circular disc 200mm diameter x 8mm thick, wood-tone color, with a center through-hole 8.3mm diameter (0.3mm clearance over Part A's pin), and 8 trapezoidal pocket recesses cut into its top face arranged radially like pie slices, each pocket 20mm wide x 40mm long x 5mm deep, with the numbers 1-8 engraved beside each pocket. A single fixed arrow 10mm long is molded onto Part A's top face at the rim, pointing inward, to serve as the alignment reference. PART C 'goods tile' (produce 48 copies, 12 each in 4 colors: orange, blue, purple, green): flat rectangular chip 18mm x 38mm x 4mm thick, engraved with a number 1-4. PART D 'claim board' (produce 4 copies, one each in red, blue, green, yellow): flat rectangular mat 100mm x 60mm x 4mm thick with 8 shallow divots 6mm diameter x 4mm deep arranged in a row numbered 1-8, and an integral upright wall 15mm tall x 3mm thick running along 3 of the 4 edges (leaving the edge nearest the player open). PART E 'claim peg' (produce 4 copies, matching Part D colors): cone shape, 10mm diameter base tapering to a rounded top, 15mm tall. PART F 'rotation die': cube 16mm x 16mm x 16mm with pips engraved on faces reading 1,1,2,2,3,3. PART G 'game box': open-top rectangular tray 260mm x 260mm x 55mm deep, wall thickness 3mm, teal color. PART H 'box lid': rectangular shell 262mm x 262mm x 8mm deep, friction-fits over Part G at 0.4mm clearance. Assembly: Part B rotates freely on Part A's pin at 0.3mm clearance, no fasteners; all tiles, pegs, and die sit loose; lid H friction-fits over box G at 0.4mm clearance.

ideas.title: Foghorn
ideas.concept: A 4-player trick-taking game where whoever wins a trick immediately spins a shared trump dial to set trump for the NEXT trick only, so every trick you win is also a public decision that tips your hand to the table. A turn feels like a card game and a bluffing game at once: you're reading what trump the last winner picked as much as you're reading the cards on the table.
ideas.differentiation: Base mechanic is standard fixed-trump trick-taking (e.g. Bridge/Spades). Searched 'trick taking game where trump suit changes every trick set by a rotating dial spun by trick winner' and the plain title 'Foghorn board game': no shipped trick-taking game titled Foghorn was found. The closest dynamic-trump comparable surfaced was Sea Change, whose trump suit changes automatically whenever a player plays a card matching the rank just played — an automatic rules-trigger, not a player choice. This idea's mechanism (the trick WINNER deliberately spins a physical dial to choose the next trump, as an explicit strategic decision made in public) is a distinct control-based twist not covered by Sea Change's automatic trigger or by standard fixed trump; treat the Sea Change comparison as the nearest partial match and this twist's player-agency-over-trump-choice as the point of difference.
ideas.rules: 4 players (3-player variant: remove one full suit, using only 36 tiles). SETUP: shuffle the 48 suit tiles (4 suits x 12, numbered 1-12) and deal 12 to each player's personal rack. Roll a 4-sided assignment (or simply have the dealer choose) to set the trump dial to a starting suit. Each player takes an empty trick collection tray. TURN: the player to the dealer's left leads any one tile from their rack face-up to the center. Going clockwise, each other player must play a tile of the led suit if they hold one; if they hold none of the led suit, they may play any tile, including the current trump suit. Once all 4 tiles are played: if any trump-suit tile was played, the highest-numbered trump tile wins the trick; otherwise the highest-numbered tile of the led suit wins. The trick winner: (a) collects all 4 played tiles face-down into their own collection tray (each worth 1 point at game end), and (b) immediately rotates the trump dial to point at any suit of their choice (including re-selecting the same suit), which becomes trump for the next trick only. The trick winner then leads the next trick. END: after all 12 tricks are played (rack empty), each player scores 1 point per tile in their collection tray. Highest score wins; ties won by whoever led the final trick.
ideas.components: 1 trump dial assembly: a 100x100x10mm flat base plaque with a fixed arrow molded on its rim and 4 alignment tick marks at 90-degree intervals, plus a rotating 80mm diameter x 6mm thick disc divided into 4 colored quadrants (red/blue/green/yellow, one per suit) mounted on a central 5mm diameter integral pivot pin. 48 suit tiles, rectangular engraved chips 30x45x4mm, 12 per suit in that suit's color, numbered 1-12. 4 player racks, angled trays 200x40x30mm with a 10mm back lip, one per player color, holding up to 8 tiles visible only to that player. 1 trick collection tray, shallow rectangular tray 100x100x10mm, grey PLA. 1 lidded box, 220x220x60mm, dark blue PLA.
ideas.producibility_notes: 4 part types (dial assembly, tiles, racks, collection tray) and a controlled 5-color palette (4 suit colors + grey/navy). The trump dial deliberately omits snap detents in favor of eyeballed alignment against a fixed printed arrow and 4 tick marks, removing the smallest-feature detent-notch risk entirely while keeping the proven pivot-disc-on-pin joint (5.3mm bore over 5mm pin, 0.3mm clearance). All other parts are flat trays/racks with no joints. No feature under 1mm.

ideas.title: Seam Works
ideas.concept: All players drill into the same shared quarry board at once, and any corridor tile you place can complete someone else's path to an ore vein just as easily as your own — so every placement is a race to be the one whose tile finally connects an ore deposit back to an entrance. A turn feels like a tense shared puzzle where you're constantly recalculating who benefits from your move.
ideas.differentiation: Searched 'underground mining tile laying game where players drill corridor tiles into a shared quarry board' and the plain title 'Seam Works board game': the closest matches were Gold Mine (tile-laying maze game where each element is a shared maze but players move individual pawns to collect gold and exit, scored by exit order/collection, not by network-connection-back-to-entrance) and Fault! (a contract/gem economy mining game with cave-in risk, no tile-laying corridor network at all). Neither uses this idea's specific win condition — a shared single board where ANY player's tile placement can trigger ANY other player's ore claim the instant a connected path exists back to that ore's original placer's fixed entrance — which is closer to a connection/network-race mechanic than to either comparable's collection-and-exit or contract-economy structure; this specific combination was not found in the results.
ideas.rules: 2-4 players. SETUP: place the shared hexagonal quarry board (37 hex sockets). Seat each player's fixed entrance base tile into their assigned edge socket (4 entrance positions pre-marked on the board, use only as many as there are players). Shuffle the remaining 76 corridor tiles (20 of which bear an ore-nugget icon) into the draw tumbler. TURN (clockwise): draw one tile blind from the tumbler, then place it face-up into any currently-open hex socket that is adjacent to at least one already-placed tile (yours or an opponent's); placement is mandatory if any legal spot exists. Immediately after placing, check every ore-nugget tile on the board: if there now exists an unbroken chain of tiles with connecting open edges running from that ore tile all the way to the entrance tile of the player who ORIGINALLY placed it, the player who just placed the connecting tile (whoever completes the chain, which may be a different player than the one who placed the ore tile) claims it immediately: flip the ore tile face-down (it stops counting for future connections) and take a matching ore token. Continue until the tumbler is empty and no legal placement remains for any player. SCORING: each ore token is worth 1 point; highest total wins; ties broken by whoever claimed an ore token most recently.
ideas.components: 1 shared quarry board, 350mm point-to-point flat hexagonal PLA board, dark grey, with 37 shallow hex sockets (45mm flat-to-flat x 3mm deep) in a honeycomb arrangement, plus 4 raised hex entrance nubs in 4 player colors fixed at 4 rim positions, plus a 30-space score track engraved around the outer edge. 80 corridor tiles, hex tiles 44x44x6mm (0.5mm clearance to sockets) engraved with corridor path patterns connecting between 2 and 6 of the hex's edges; 20 of these additionally bear a raised ore-nugget bump (6mm dia x 2mm tall). 4 entrance base tiles, hex tiles matching the corridor footprint, pre-printed with each player's color/symbol. 1 draw tumbler, opaque drum 90mm dia x 70mm tall with a 32mm snap-fit flip lid. 4 score markers, pyramid pegs 15x15x15mm, one per player color. 1 lidded box, 380x380x70mm, dark grey PLA.
ideas.producibility_notes: 5 part types (board, corridor tiles, entrance tiles, tumbler, score markers) and 5 colors (4 player + grey). All tiles are flat hexagonal prisms sitting in shallow sockets with a stated 0.5mm clearance, no interlocking pegs or edge-matching pins required (edges are read visually by the printed corridor pattern, not by a physical connector), which removes any tile-to-tile joint tolerance risk entirely. The only joint is the tumbler's snap-fit lid, same proven class as other ideas in this batch. No feature under 1mm; smallest feature is the 2mm-tall ore bump.

ideas.title: Canal Locks
ideas.concept: A 2-player canal-engineering race where you and your rival take turns snapping little canal-segment rods between fixed junction pegs, and completing the fourth side of any square immediately hands you that lock-chamber and an extra turn. It plays exactly like a childhood pencil game but every line is a physical rod you press-fit into place.
ideas.differentiation: Base game is the classic public-domain pencil game Dots and Boxes (19th century, Edouard Lucas), confirmed via direct search of its Wikipedia entry and multiple digital ports. This is a pure styling reskin: identical ruleset (claim the 4th edge of a 1x1 cell to score it and go again), restyled as Dutch canal-lock engineering with physical peg-and-rod connectors replacing pencil lines and square roof-cap tokens replacing pencil-drawn boxes. Searched 'dots and boxes game canal locks Amsterdam theme board game' and the plain title 'Canal Locks board game' directly: no existing product combines Dots and Boxes with a canal/lock theme (results returned only an unrelated Amsterdam canal-house building game, Canal Houses, with no line-drawing mechanic).
ideas.rules: 2 players. SETUP: place the canal grid board (36 peg nubs in a 6x6 grid). Each player takes an unlimited-use pool of their color's rod connectors (from the shared 60-rod supply) and roof-cap tokens (13 for one player, 12 for the other in a standard 5x5-cell grid, adjust supply to match total cells). TURN: press-fit one rod connector between any two adjacent peg nubs that are not already connected. If that rod completes all 4 sides of any 1x1 grid cell, snap your color's roof-cap token onto that completed cell and take another turn (place another rod); if it completes no cell, your turn ends. Continue until every possible adjacent-peg connection (60 total edges in the 6x6 grid) has a rod. SCORING: count roof-cap tokens; the player with more claimed lock-chambers (of the 25 total 1x1 cells) wins; a tie is a draw.

ideas.producibility_notes: 3 part types (board, rods, roof caps) and a minimal 3-color palette (board blue + 2 player colors). The rod-to-peg joint is a straightforward peg-in-hole press-fit stated at a 0.2mm interference (3.2mm hole for a 3mm pin), the same proven joint family used elsewhere in this batch, just applied twice per rod. No feature under 1mm; smallest feature is the 3mm connector pins.

ideas.title: Loom Weave
ideas.concept: A classic mill-formation duel restyled as competing weavers on a loom-shaped board, where lining up three of your spool-shaped bobbins removes one of your opponent's threads from play. It plays exactly like the ancient strategy game it's built on, just dressed as a textile duel.
ideas.differentiation: Base game is the classic public-domain Nine Men's Morris (confirmed via direct search: 24-point board, place-then-move phases, form a mill of 3-in-a-row to remove an opponent piece, flying rule at 3 pieces remaining). This is a pure styling reskin: identical ruleset, restyled with a loom-frame-shaped board and spool/bobbin-shaped pegs replacing flat disc pieces. Searched 'nine men's morris mill game weaving loom textile theme board game' and the plain title 'Loom Weave board game' directly: no existing product combines Nine Men's Morris with a weaving/loom theme (results returned only standard wood/travel editions of Nine Men's Morris itself, no textile-themed variant).
ideas.rules: 2 players, 9 bobbins each (cream vs burgundy). PHASE 1 (placing): players alternate placing 1 bobbin from hand onto any empty point of the 24-point board (3 concentric squares connected by 4 midpoint lines, standard Nine Men's Morris layout). If a placement completes a 'weave' (3 of that player's own bobbins in an unbroken straight line along a printed board line), that player immediately removes 1 opponent bobbin of their choice from the board (a bobbin that is part of an opponent's already-formed weave may not be removed unless no other opponent bobbin is available). PHASE 2 (moving): once all 18 bobbins are placed, players alternate moving 1 of their own bobbins along a printed line to an adjacent empty point; forming or reforming a weave again triggers an opponent-bobbin removal under the same rule. SPECIAL RULE: once a player is reduced to exactly 3 bobbins remaining, that player may 'fly' — moving any one bobbin to any empty point on the board regardless of adjacency, on their turn. WIN CONDITION: a player wins immediately by reducing the opponent to 2 bobbins, or by leaving the opponent with no legal move on their turn.
ideas.components: 1 loom board, 240x240x8mm flat rectangular PLA board with a printed frame border, engraved with the standard 24-point Nine Men's Morris grid pattern (3 concentric squares plus 4 connecting midpoint lines) as printed lines, and 24 shallow holes (8mm dia x 6mm deep) at each grid point. 18 bobbin pegs, spool-shaped pieces (two 12mm dia discs joined by a 6mm dia x 15mm tall waist, overall 22mm tall, peg base 7.8mm dia to fit board holes), 9 in cream PLA and 9 in burgundy PLA. 1 lidded box, 260x260x50mm, burgundy PLA.

The bobbin-to-hole fit is a straightforward peg-in-hole joint stated at 0.2mm clearance (8mm hole for a 7.8mm peg base). No feature under 1mm; the spool waist at 6mm diameter is well above the minimum printable feature size.

ideas.title: Lantern Keepers
ideas.concept: A fully cooperative game where you and your fellow keepers share one rotating lighthouse beacon and can only illuminate a single shipping lane at a time, while ships in the dark lanes keep drifting toward the rocks. A round feels like triage: you physically spin the light toward whichever lane is about to lose a ship, knowing the other three lanes are creeping closer to disaster while you do.
ideas.differentiation: Searched 'cooperative lighthouse game rotating beacon disc guiding ships away from rocks' and the plain title 'Lantern Keepers board game': the only lighthouse-titled shipped product found was The Last Lighthouse (Button Shy, 2024), which was checked directly — it is a solo card-only game about surviving a Nightmare-card deck with Trap cards, containing no beacon-rotation mechanic, no ships, no rocks-approach-track, and no cooperative multiplayer mode. No shipped game combining a single shared rotating beacon that can protect only one of several simultaneously-advancing ship lanes was found in any result.
ideas.rules: 2-4 players, fully cooperative, ends in a shared win or shared loss. SETUP: place the harbor board (4 lanes, each with 6 track stops running from 'open sea' to 'rocks'). Place 2 ship pegs on the outermost 'open sea' stop of each of the 4 lanes (8 ships total). Set the beacon disc to illuminate any 1 starting lane. Set the shipwreck tracker to 0. ROUND (repeat until win/loss): (1) Beacon Phase — the active player (rotates clockwise each round) may rotate the beacon disc to point at any 1 of the 4 lanes, or leave it where it is. (2) Advance Phase — for each of the 3 lanes NOT currently illuminated: every ship peg in that lane advances 1 stop toward the rocks. For the 1 illuminated lane: every ship peg in it instead advances 1 stop toward the harbor (the opposite direction, representing being guided to safety); if a ship peg reaches the harbor-side stop, remove it from the board and score 1 point. (3) Wreck Check — any ship peg that reaches the rocks-side final stop of its lane (from advancing in the dark) is wrecked: remove it from the board and advance the shipwreck tracker by 1. WIN CONDITION: the group wins immediately once 8 total ships have been safely docked at the harbor. LOSS CONDITION: the group loses immediately if the shipwreck tracker reaches 6.
ideas.components: 1 harbor board, 300x200x10mm flat rectangular PLA board (dark blue) depicting 4 curved lane tracks converging on an integral central lighthouse pillar (20mm dia x 50mm tall) at one edge, each lane printed with 6 discrete stop divots (10mm dia x 3mm deep) running from open-sea to rocks, plus a 10-space shipwreck track with a peg marker along one edge. 1 beacon disc, 60mm dia x 8mm thick disc with a printed 45-degree yellow light-cone wedge, mounted on the lighthouse pillar's 6mm dia through-hole as its pivot. 8 ship pegs, small boat-shaped pieces 15x8x10mm with a 6mm dia x 5mm tall base peg, grey PLA. 20 shipwreck tokens, flat red discs 12mm dia x 3mm thick. 1 shipwreck tracker peg, 8mm dia x 15mm tall cylinder, red PLA. 1 lidded box, 320x220x60mm, dark blue PLA.
ideas.producibility_notes: 6 part types (board+pillar as one piece, beacon disc, ship pegs, shipwreck tokens, tracker peg, box) and a controlled 4-color palette (dark blue, yellow accent, grey ships, red tracker). The beacon disc is the proven pivot-disc joint, stated with a 6.3mm bore over the board's integral 6mm pillar-top pin (0.3mm clearance, free-spinning, no detents needed since only 4 lane positions need rough visual alignment against printed lane-entrance markers on the board). All ship/track movement is discrete divot-to-divot by hand, fully deterministic with no physical balance or gravity-feed risk. No feature under 1mm.

ideas.title: Flagline
ideas.concept: A silent relay game where a secret word gets passed down a line of players purely through the angle of two rotating semaphore-style flag arms on each player's signal board, with no talking allowed until the last player calls out their answer. It turns the childhood whisper-down-the-lane game into a tense visual-copying puzzle where one misread angle sinks the whole word.
ideas.differentiation: Base structure is the classic folk party game Whisper Down the Lane / Telephone (a message relayed player-to-player with information loss at each step, no single publisher/owner). Searched 'cooperative party game where players relay a hidden message down a line using rotating semaphore flag pegs at fixed angle positions' and the plain title 'Flagline board game': results returned only educational/scouting semaphore-teaching resources and unrelated flag-trivia board games (Flags of the World, Flags The Game), none of which are relay games at all, let alone one using physical semaphore encoding as the entire information channel. The specific twist — replacing spoken whispering with a fixed-vocabulary physical semaphore encoding relayed purely by visual copying of rotating flag-arm angles, with only the first and last players holding a decoder key — is not documented in any shipped product found.
ideas.rules: 4-6 players, fully cooperative, played seated in a line in a fixed order. SETUP: give the first and last player in line each an identical code-key tile (a chart mapping the 64 possible two-arm angle combinations to a fixed list of 30 words). Every player, including the first and last, also receives a blank signal board with 2 independently rotating flag-arm pegs. Shuffle the 30 message tiles into a face-down draw stack next to the first player. ROUND: the first player draws the top message tile, secretly reads the word on it, looks up its matching angle combination on their code-key tile, and rotates their own 2 flag-arm pegs to that exact combination (each arm clicks into 1 of 8 fixed 45-degree positions). Once set, the first player announces 'ready' and holds their board still. The second player studies the first player's board and, using the removable privacy screen to block it from the third player, sets their own flag-arm pegs to match the exact same 2 angles purely by copying what they see (no verbal hints, no consulting a code-key, since only the first and last player have one). This repeats down the line, each player copying only the board immediately before theirs. When the last player receives the final board, they read its 2 flag-arm angles, look up the matching word on their own code-key tile, and say the word aloud. SCORING: if the announced word matches the original message tile, the team scores 1 point and sets the tile aside as a keep; if not, the tile is discarded. Play continues, drawing a new message tile each round, until the draw stack (30 tiles) is exhausted. TEAM WIN CONDITION: the team wins if they score at least 20 correct words out of 30 (adjust threshold for a harder or easier game).
ideas.components: 5 signal boards, flat rectangular PLA boards 100x140x10mm, one per player, each with 2 independently rotating flag-arm pegs mounted on 2 fixed integral pivot pins (6mm dia x 8mm tall, spaced 40mm apart); each flag-arm is a flat paddle 8x35x3mm attached to a rotating hub (12mm dia x 6mm tall) with a small triangular detent nub (1.5mm tall) on its underside clicking into 8 matching notches (1.5mm deep) printed in a ring on the board around each pivot pin, giving 8 fixed 45-degree stops per arm. 2 code-key tiles, rigid engraved reference boards 120x180x4mm, printed with a grid mapping all 64 two-arm angle combinations to a fixed list of 30 words. 30 message tiles, flat chips 40x40x3mm, each engraved with one word from the fixed vocabulary, face-down in a stack. 5 privacy screens, flat standing panels 100x60x2mm with a small tab that clips into a slot on the edge of any signal board. 1 lidded box, 260x180x60mm, dark green PLA.
ideas.producibility_notes: 5 part types (signal boards, flag-arm pegs as a sub-part of the boards, code-key tiles, message tiles, privacy screens) but a high joint count (10 total flag-arm pivots across 5 boards), which is the batch's highest-risk design and was deliberately NOT chosen as a build pick for that reason. Every pivot uses the proven pivot-disc-with-detents joint family, explicitly dimensioned: 6.3mm hub bore over a 6mm integral pin (0.3mm clearance) and a 1.5mm detent nub/notch pair, kept at or above the 1mm minimum-feature threshold. The privacy screen's clip-in tab is a simple slot-and-tab friction fit, also explicitly dimensioned.

PART D 'privacy screen' (produce 5 copies, dark green color): a flat standing panel 100mm wide x 60mm tall x 2mm thick with a rectangular tab 55mm long x 2mm thick x 4mm deep protruding from its bottom edge, sized to slide into Part A's edge slot with 0.3mm clearance for a snug but removable friction fit. PART E 'message tile' (produce 30 copies, tan color): flat square chip 40mm x 40mm x 3mm thick, engraved with one word. PART F 'game box': open-top rectangular tray 260mm x 180mm x 55mm deep, wall thickness 3mm, dark green. PART G 'box lid': rectangular shell 262mm x 182mm x 8mm deep, friction-fits over Part F at 0.4mm clearance. Assembly: Part B hubs mount on Part A's pins at 0.3mm clearance and rotate by hand, clicking between the 8 detent notches via the 1.5mm nub; Part D's tab slides into Part A's edge slot at 0.3mm clearance, removable; lid G friction-fits over box F at 0.4mm clearance.

cad_build_picks.reason: Cipher Row uses only single-depth peg-in-hole joints (no layered holes, no snap detents beyond one simple clear-cap friction fit) across a tightly controlled 6-color palette, and its twist mechanic is fully resolved on the physical board itself with no ambiguous or optional-sounding geometry for the CAD pipeline to misinterpret.

Threshing Floor's central stacking mechanic is deterministic by construction (rigid integral posts, not a balance/dexterity risk) with only 5 part types and 5 colors total, making it the lowest-fidelity-risk build in the batch to compare against its own concept and components list.

Foghorn deliberately drops snap-detents from its pivot-disc joint in favor of a fixed-arrow visual-alignment design, giving it the fewest tolerance-dependent features of any twist idea in the batch while still showcasing a genuine, differentiated rule change.
